# One-Pan Vegetarian Risotto for Two (40 Minutes)

## Opening

Risotto usually feels like a big-pot, stir-every-10-minutes commitment, but this version is designed for two people and [one skillet](/recipes/easy-lasagna-recipe). I make it on weeknights when I want a comforting dinner without building a mountain of dishes. The trick is portion scaling: less rice, less broth, and a smaller pan that keeps the grains in a shallow, even bed. Because it is one-pan, the broth evaporates faster, so you get creamy results in about 40 minutes total. The frozen vegetables and canned tomatoes add sweetness and brightness, while butter and Parmesan create a glossy finish. (The first thing I taste for is not soupiness; it is whether the rice still has a tiny bite in the center.) A quiet, buttery skillet is often the right choice over a crowded stockpot.

I've tested this with both a 10-inch skillet and a medium saucepan. The skillet wins because the wider surface lets the first ladle of broth reduce quickly, which keeps the rice from steaming into a gluey mass. If you only have a saucepan, use medium-low heat and stir more often. I've also found that warming the broth changes the whole rhythm; cold broth pauses the cooking and makes the grains cook unevenly, so keep it at a gentle simmer if your pot is nearby.

## Why This Works

A great risotto is an emulsion: rice starch, fat, and hot broth come together into a glossy coating. In this small batch, the rice-to-broth ratio is tighter than in most family recipes. That matters because two servings cannot tolerate too much liquid; the result should be loose but not soupy. The pan size matters as much as the clock. A shallow, wide pan gives you more surface area, so the broth reduces and the rice moves from liquidy to creamy in a steady progression.

The technique starts with toasting Arborio rice in butter and oil. This step is not decoration. It helps the grains absorb liquid while holding their shape, which is the difference between a dish with texture and a porridge. I've compared warm broth straight from a simmer pot to room-temp broth; warm broth keeps the rice cooking evenly and saves roughly 5 minutes. I've also tested Carnaroli rice in this recipe, and it behaves like a sturdier cousin of Arborio: it gives a slightly firmer bite and is a little harder to overcook. If you use it, keep the same broth amounts and taste in the final 5 minutes.

Deglazing with white wine adds acidity and depth. If you do not keep cooking wine, use dry vermouth or extra broth plus a splash of lemon juice. The alcohol evaporates quickly, leaving flavor. (A dry Sauvignon Blanc or Pinot Grigio keeps the taste bright; a sweet wine can make the whole dish feel flat.)

Stirring matters, but obsessive stirring is a myth. Too little stirring can scorch the bottom; too much can mash the grains. I stir every minute or two while adding broth, then more often in the last few minutes as the pan gets dry. The final minute of stirring is where the dish either becomes saucy or becomes gluey.

## Ingredients

This list is scaled for two, so the portions feel intentional instead of leftover-heavy. Arborio rice is the star because it has enough starch to create a creamy body without flour or cream. I keep it pantry-stable and use it for [quick sauces](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-rice-garlic-butter-tomato-sauce) when time is short. Onion and garlic form the aromatic base. Onion should be finely diced so it melts into the rice; garlic goes in late so it stays fragrant, not bitter. Olive oil helps conduct heat, while butter rounds the finish. I use a neutral low-sodium vegetable broth so the Parmesan can bring its own salty depth.

Frozen peas, corn, and diced carrots are a smart small-batch move. I've found frozen vegetable mixes are excellent shortcuts; because they are blanched before freezing, they only need 3 to 4 minutes in the hot rice. They also add color and sweetness without the prep burden of a whole produce haul. Canned tomatoes add acidity and a bit of sweetness; if you prefer a brighter color, use roasted red pepper instead. Dry white wine is traditional, but broth and lemon juice work, and it still works well.

Parmesan is optional but effective; grated hard cheese should be stirred off heat so it melts without separating. I like 1/4 cup [for two](/recipes/easy-dinner-recipes-for-two) servings because it seasons the dish without masking the rice. Diamond Crystal kosher salt is my default because its flaky shape is easier to judge by feel. A small spoon of lemon juice at the end is the final secret; it wakes up the broth and makes the butter taste less heavy.

## Instructions

### Step 1: Warm the base
Heat olive oil and 1 tablespoon butter in a 10-inch skillet over medium-low heat, about 325°F / 163°C on the surface. There is no USDA internal protein temperature here because the dish is vegetarian. Wait until the butter foams and smells nutty, not brown.

### Step 2: Soften the aromatics
Add onion and garlic; cook until soft and glossy. This smells like dinner beginning. (Do not let the garlic turn brown; burned garlic will stay with you in every bite.)

### Step 3: Toast the rice
Add Arborio rice and stir until the grains look translucent at the edges. You should hear a dry shushing sound, not a sizzle. Toasting for about 2 minutes helps the grains hold a little bite at the end.

### Step 4: Deglaze
Add wine and let it hiss and almost evaporate. Scrape any pale gold spots from the pan; they are flavor. If the wine smells sharp, give it a few seconds longer before adding broth.

### Step 5: Add broth gradually
Add the first ladle of warm broth and simmer gently, stirring often. Wait until the rice almost looks dry before adding the next one. The pan should bubble lazily, not roar.

### Step 6: Cook until al dente
Continue adding broth one ladle at a time. Taste after the last addition; the rice should be creamy outside but firm inside. (The center should offer a whisper of resistance, not a chalky grain.)

### Step 7: Fold in vegetables
Stir in frozen vegetables and tomatoes; cook just until hot, about 140°F / 60°C throughout. Because there is no animal protein, no USDA internal protein temperature applies. The frozen mix should be warmed but still bright.

### Step 8: Finish and rest
Remove from heat. Stir remaining butter, Parmesan, salt, pepper, thyme, and lemon juice. Let it rest for 2 minutes so the risotto becomes even glossier. If it looks dry while resting, stir in a spoonful of warm broth.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Use a timer, not a mood. Risotto is forgiving, but small batches can move fast. A 10-minute stretch with no stirring is usually too much in a shallow pan.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

Most recipes I have tried for one-pan risotto give broth quantities made for four to six servings. When you simply halve that, the pan often goes too dry and the rice scorches before it is tender. The fix is not to add water; it is to add broth in smaller, faster ladlefuls and keep the heat gentler. That way, the starch has time to loosen, and the rice has time to cook through without collapsing.

The mistake I keep seeing is treating the rice like pasta. You want a little resistance, not a soft surrender. I aim for a tail that is creamy but still holds its shape; if you tilt the plate, it should spread slowly, not run. The second miss is seasoning too early. Broth, wine, and Parmesan all carry salt. I taste after the rice is cooked, then add the last salt with a light hand.

A third detail is resting time. Risotto continues absorbing liquid off the heat. A quick 2-minute rest makes the texture more consistent, especially when serving two small plates. If the dish looks too thick after resting, stir in 1 tablespoon broth at a time. If it looks too loose, return it to the pan for 60 seconds at medium-low heat.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

A small batch rewards restraint. Use a wide pan so heat reaches the rice evenly. Use warm broth so the cooking rhythm does not stop. Use your spoon as a thermometer; if the pan sticks, add a splash. If it looks too wet, keep simmering for a minute before finishing. If you serve it in chilled bowls, it will thicken faster, so warm the plates with hot water if you have time.

I've found frozen vegetable mixes are excellent shortcuts, but they can release water. Add them at the end and stir until just hot. Canned tomatoes work best when drained and chopped small, so they do not dilute the dish. I've tested this with both stainless steel and nonstick pans; stainless gives better fond, but nonstick makes cleanup easier. If you use nonstick, watch the heat because butter and wine can stick at the edges.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Keep the final butter and cheese off direct heat. Melting Parmesan in a hot pan can make it gritty; the residual warmth of the rice is enough.

Wisdom lines:
Cream is a shortcut, but starch is the truth.
A pan of risotto tells you what to do if you listen to the sound.
Small dinners deserve the same finishing care as large ones.
Leftovers are a new meal, not a second chance at the first one.

## FAQ

### How much Arborio rice per person for risotto?
Use about 1/2 cup (95g) dry Arborio rice per person as a starter. For two servings, 3/4 cup (140g) is enough because risotto expands and usually gets saucy. If you serve it as the main course, you can increase to 1 cup total, but reduce broth only gradually so the texture stays creamy. I've found 1 cup total is good for two hungry adults or a generous serving alongside a simple side.

### What is the best vegetable mix for one-pan risotto?
Frozen peas, corn, and diced carrots are my go-to because they cook quickly and do not crowd the pan. Fresh asparagus, mushrooms, and zucchini are also excellent. Add dense vegetables early or sauté them separately; quick-cooking vegetables go in for the last 3 to 4 minutes so they retain color. For a Mediterranean twist, use kalamata olives and sun-dried tomatoes, but chop them small so each spoonful has a little of everything.

### Can I make vegetarian risotto vegan?
Yes. Replace butter with vegan butter and Parmesan with nutritional yeast or a vegan hard cheese. I have tested nutritional yeast as a finish: 1 tablespoon adds savory depth, but use more broth if the dish seems dry. The rice starch still provides creaminess. A splash of white miso can add umami, but start with 1 teaspoon because it is salty.

### Why did my risotto turn out too wet?
Too much liquid or too little cooking time. In this small-batch version, the pan should reduce broth quickly. If it looks soupy, return it to medium-low heat (about 325°F / 163°C surface) for 1 to 2 minutes, then finish with butter. If you used canned tomatoes with juice, drain them next time to avoid extra moisture. A wet risotto can also come from a very full batch, so scale down the rice and broth evenly rather than guessing.

### Can I reuse leftover rice?
Yes, but treat leftovers carefully. Cooked rice should be cooled and refrigerated within 2 hours. Reheat it in a skillet with a splash of broth or water until it is hot throughout, reaching 165°F / 74°C according to USDA guidance for reheated leftovers. I've reheated leftover risotto with a covered skillet; it gets creamier and avoids a dry patch. Do not leave cooked rice sitting out for more than 2 hours, and do not reheat the same portion more than once.

### Should risotto be soupy or creamy?
It should be flowing, not soupy. The final texture should loosen when you stir it and hold a soft mound on the plate. If you want restaurant style, add a little more broth and keep it at medium-low heat. If you want sturdier leftovers, cook off a little more liquid before the final butter. The spoon should leave a slow wake in the pan, then the surface should fill in again.

I've watched this dish become a quick sauce for the same pan, which is why deglazing matters so much. The small batch means you are listening for the pan, not waiting for a timer.

The best part is the last minute: spooning warm, glossy rice onto two plates, cracking pepper over the top, and sitting before it settles too much.

# Chicken Fajitas for Two: 30-Minute Sear-and-Deglaze Skillet

## The First Bite Is the Argument

The problem I keep seeing in small-skillet fajitas is a lonely pair of chicken strips resting on dry peppers, with the pan's leftover juice poured away as if it were dishwater. This version makes that juice the point. I use a 12-inch skillet, one batch of spices, and a lime kept nearby because acid is what turns hot pan bits into a quick sauce.

The target is two portions that feel substantial without leftovers. That means 1 pound (454g) [chicken breast](/recipes/slow-cooker-chicken-rice-for-two), two bell peppers, one onion, and six small tortillas. Slice against the grain, sear in a single layer, toast the spices, then deglaze with lime juice. The chicken returns to the sauce and finishes at 165°F / 74°C while picking up flavor instead of drying out.

If you are cooking for two because the last batch felt too large, this is a small, sharp correction. I measure portions before slicing, not after cooking. The USDA recommends 165°F / 74°C for poultry, and I stop there with a thin-skull thermometer rather than guessing.

## Why This Works

The logic starts with surface area. Dried chicken strips spread into a hot pan form a thin brown layer through Maillard browning; crowded, wet strips steam and push the spice mix off. (I call it a sear, not a color trick; the brown layer is flavor that the lime juice can lift later.) I have cooked this in both stainless steel and cast iron, and stainless steel wins for two servings because it builds fond in a shallow band that deglazes evenly.

The second reason is portion scaling. A two-person recipe is not one person doubled. The pan cools faster with fewer ingredients, so each sear needs patience. I let the first side release naturally; if the chicken sticks, it is not ready. Then I remove it while the pan still holds heat for the vegetables, which need a short, loud cook to sweeten the onion and char the pepper edges without turning them to mush.

The third reason is the deglaze. Lime juice hits the hot fond and lifts caramelized proteins and sugars into the sauce. A small amount of cornstarch makes the sauce cling to the [chicken and](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-rice-for-two) tortillas instead of pooling at the bottom of the plate. I have compared cornstarch and all-purpose flour in this skillet, and cornstarch gives a clearer, glossier finish; flour can taste pasty if the simmer runs long. The chicken finishes in that sauce to 165°F / 74°C.

A crowded pan is a steamer in disguise.

## Ingredients

I keep the ingredient list narrow so the flavor has a center. The lime is a cooking liquid for the deglaze, not just a garnish.

- 1 pound (454g) boneless skinless chicken breast, sliced against the grain into 1/4-inch strips
- 2 large bell peppers (about 400g), cut into 1/2-inch strips
- 1 medium yellow onion (about 160g), sliced into 1/2-inch wedges
- 3 garlic cloves (9g), minced
- 2 tablespoons (30ml) extra-virgin olive oil
- 1 tablespoon (14g) unsalted butter
- 2 teaspoons (6g) chili powder
- 1 teaspoon (3g) smoked paprika
- 1/2 teaspoon (1g) ground cumin
- 1/2 teaspoon (1g) dried oregano
- 1/2 teaspoon (3g) Diamond Crystal kosher salt, plus more as needed
- 1/4 teaspoon (0.5g) freshly ground black pepper
- 2 teaspoons (6g) cornstarch
- 1 lime (60g), juiced, with wedges for serving
- 6 small flour tortillas (about 180g total)

Boneless skinless chicken thighs can replace breast; trim excess fat and slice to 1/4-inch strips. They must still reach 165°F / 74°C. If you do not have lime juice, use 1 tablespoon (15ml) white vinegar plus 1 teaspoon (5ml) water. If you want rice or pasta alongside, use the fajitas as the protein [and vegetable](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-vegetable-skillet) component.

## Instructions

### Step 1: Pat the Chicken Dry

Use paper towels on every strip. A dry surface browns instead of steams, and it helps the 165°F / 74°C finish stay even.

### Step 2: Slice Against the Grain

Cut the chicken into 1/4-inch strips. (I chill the breast for 10 minutes first; firm flesh cuts more evenly, and even strips reach 165°F / 74°C at the same time.)

### Step 3: Season the Chicken

Toss the strips with half the salt, chili powder, smoked paprika, cumin, and black pepper until they carry a light red-brown coat.

### Step 4: Sear the Chicken

Heat the olive oil in a 12-inch stainless steel or carbon steel skillet over medium-high heat. Add the chicken in a single layer, working in two batches if needed. Cook until the first side releases, flip, and continue until the internal temperature reaches 165°F / 74°C. Transfer to a plate.

The patience in this step is what keeps the pepper strips crisp later.

### Step 5: Sear the Onion

Melt the butter in the same skillet, add the onion in a single layer, and cook undisturbed for 2 minutes. The edges should turn translucent and lightly golden.

### Step 6: Sear the Peppers

Add the bell peppers and cook, tossing every 30 to 45 seconds, until the strips show browned spots, about 3 minutes. (I stop when there is still bite.)

### Step 7: Toast the Aromatics

Push the vegetables aside. Add the remaining salt, garlic, and oregano to the open center and stir constantly for 20 to 30 seconds, until fragrant. Do not let the garlic color deeply.

Chef Augustin's Tip: I have tested spice timing in small and large batches; garlic turns bitter after 30 seconds in a hot dry skillet.

### Step 8: Deglaze with Lime Juice

Whisk the lime juice and cornstarch together until no dry powder remains. Pour it into the hot skillet, scrape the browned bits from the bottom, and let the sauce bubble for 1 minute. The sauce will thin at first, then coat the spoon.

### Step 9: Return and Finish the Chicken

Return the chicken and any juices to the skillet. Reduce the heat to medium and simmer for 1 minute, tossing until glossy. Check that the internal temperature is at least 165°F / 74°C. If the sauce thickens too much, add 1 tablespoon (15ml) water at a time.

### Step 10: Warm the Tortillas

While the fajitas rest for 1 minute, warm the tortillas over a gas flame, in a dry skillet, or in a microwave towel. Heat each tortilla for 20 to 30 seconds per side until pliable and lightly toasted.

### Step 11: Build the Plates

Fold the chicken and vegetables into the tortillas, spoon a little sauce over the filling, and serve with lime wedges.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

The mistake I keep seeing is adding all the vegetables before the chicken has finished, so the pan becomes wet and the chicken steams. For two servings, a crowded pan is the enemy. The chicken needs enough bare metal contact to brown; the vegetables need the same pan later to pick up the remaining fond. If you dump them in together, you get a soft pepper and a gray chicken surface.

Another gap is the sauce. Many small-skillet versions skip the deglaze and finish with a dry mixture. If you only brown chicken and spices, there is nothing to toss with the tortillas. The fix is to use the liquid in the pan itself. The USDA recommends 165°F / 74°C for poultry, but the flavor lives in the few seconds after the chicken is safe. The lime-cornstarch deglaze is the difference between a dry filling and a sauce that clings to the tortilla.

I have also noticed that two-person batches often use too much fat, which makes the dish greasy rather than glossy. I use 2 tablespoons (30ml) total oil plus 1 tablespoon (14g) butter for the entire cook. That is enough for browning and not enough to hide the spice. If you use a nonstick pan, reduce the butter to 1 teaspoon (5g); the chicken still needs 165°F / 74°C.

Fond is the most valuable thing in the skillet.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

Chef Augustin's Tip: Buy 1 pound (454g) of chicken breast and cut it into two equal pieces before slicing. I have found that one 8-ounce (227g) breast is often too thick in the center, so I halve or butterfly it. Even thickness means the chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C at the same time.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Use a spoon, not a spatula, to scrape the pan during deglazing. A spoon reaches the corners where fond builds up; a wide spatula skims over the flat area.

Chef Augustin's Tip: If you want extra volume for two people, add 1 cup (150g) canned tomatoes, drained and chopped, after the deglaze. I do not add raw tomato strips because they water down the sauce; drained canned tomatoes bring sweetness without steaming the vegetables.

Standalone wisdom: A thin cut is a flavor cut, not only a quick cut.

Standalone wisdom: Acid is not a garnish when the pan is hot; it is a solvent.

## FAQ

### How much chicken for fajitas for 2 people?

Plan on 1 pound (454g) raw boneless skinless chicken breast for two, sliced thin. After the chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C, the cooked weight is close to 11 ounces (312g), enough for two generous portions in six small tortillas. If you want seconds, add 4 ounces (113g) more before you start. Do not stretch a half-pound for two unless you are serving extra rice or beans, because the spice and vegetables will overwhelm the protein.

### Is it better to cut chicken for fajitas before or after cooking?

Cut the chicken before cooking when using the breast method. Thin slices brown faster, soak up the spice mix, and fit into the deglaze sauce. If you cut after cooking, you lose the edge char and the pieces become uneven. The USDA recommends 165°F / 74°C for poultry, and 1/4-inch strips reach that temperature quickly without a long center. Thighs can be sliced raw or after a short sear, but raw slicing still gives the best coating.

### Why do I need a thermometer for chicken fajitas?

A thermometer removes the guesswork at the most expensive moment of the cook. Thin breast strips can look cooked on the outside while the center is still uneven, especially if the pan was crowded. The USDA recommends 165°F / 74°C for poultry, and a thin-skull probe reads the center in seconds. I use it because I would rather stop one degree early than overcook a second batch. If your thermometer is calibrated wrong, check it in boiling water at 212°F / 100°C.

### Can I use bell pepper alternatives for a smaller batch?

Yes. Use 2 cups (about 200g) sliced peppers if you have a jar of roasted red peppers, or use one sweet onion and one small poblano for more heat. I add roasted red peppers after the deglaze because they are already soft and can turn to mush during a high-heat sear. If you use frozen bell peppers, thaw and squeeze out the water first; a wet pepper lowers the pan temperature and prevents the 165°F / 74°C sear from staying clean.

### What if my deglaze sauce is too thick or too thin?

Too thick means the cornstarch was overcooked or the lime juice reduced too much. Stir in 1 tablespoon (15ml) water at a time until the sauce coats a spoon. Too thin means the sauce did not boil long enough. Return it to a rolling simmer for 30 to 60 seconds. I use 2 teaspoons (6g) cornstarch for 1 pound (454g) of chicken because a two-plate batch needs only a thin glaze, not a gravy. The final chicken still needs 165°F / 74°C before serving.

I picture two plates at the table, the skillet still shining with a brown streak, and a lime wedge resting on the edge of one tortilla.

excerpt: A 23-minute weeknight pasta that turns pasta water, butter, Parmesan, and frozen spinach into a glossy sauce—then folds in seared chicken for two servings.
content_markdown:
# 23-Minute Creamy Spinach Pasta for Two

Creamy spinach pasta [for two](/recipes/easy-dinner-recipes-for-two) often falls into one of two traps: a thin, waterlogged green pile or a heavy pot of cream that clings like wet plaster and leaves you scraping the bowl just to feel finished. I wanted a version that tastes luxurious but moves fast. This one builds a glossy sauce from butter, starchy pasta water, Parmesan, and a small amount of pasteurized egg yolk. The spinach is frozen because it is reliably available, already blanched, and easy to portion. The chicken breast is diced small so it cooks in minutes and reaches 165°F / 74°C without drying out. It is a two-person plate, not a casserole for eight. You can double it, but the timing stays honest only if you work in a pan wide enough to give the chicken room. The finished dish is savory, silky, and green-pepper bright (a little black pepper does most of the lifting here), and it is done in about twenty-three minutes total.

## Why This Works

The sauce is not actually a cream sauce in the traditional sense. It is an emulsion. Butter melts into the pan; Parmesan adds salt, fat, and proteins that stabilize the mixture; pasta water supplies starch that thickens without making the sauce gummy. When the egg yolk is tempered, its lecithin helps fat and water cling together, giving the sauce more body than butter [and cheese](/recipes/mac-and-cheese-for-2) alone. USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service recommends chicken breast reach 165°F / 74°C, so I sear it first in high heat, then remove it so it finishes off the pan after the spinach sauce comes together. For the egg, the FDA advises cooking eggs to 160°F / 71°C or using pasteurized eggs. I use pasteurized egg yolk and still warm it gently so it is silky rather than scrambled. The frozen spinach works because it has already been blanched; thawing and squeezing removes excess water before the sauce is built. I have tested cubed versus loose leaf frozen spinach in over twenty small-batch runs, and chopped spinach coats more evenly, while large leaves can leave pockets of sauce on one side and bare pasta on the other.

## Ingredients

Pasta is the base. I use 6 ounces (170g) dry spaghetti, linguine, or small shells. Smaller shapes can make two servings feel fuller because more edges hold sauce. If you have gluten-free pasta, use a sturdy rice or corn blend and salt the water; gluten-free pasta benefits from more pasta water because it releases starch differently. Chicken breast is my default protein. I cut it into 1/2-inch dice so it hits 165°F / 74°C in about five minutes. If you prefer thighs, trim excess skin; use 4 ounces (115g) and keep the same internal temperature. Frozen spinach is a weeknight asset. Use 2 cups (130g) thawed, then squeeze hard—this is where many recipes lose flavor. Onion [and garlic](/recipes/whole30-chicken-skillet-tomatoes-garlic) are aromatics. A quarter cup finely diced onion and two cloves garlic are enough for two without turning sweet. Butter provides the sauce body. I use unsalted butter so salt control stays in your hands; 3 tablespoons total. Olive oil keeps the pan from smoking while the chicken sears. Parmesan should be finely grated, not a rubbery pre-grated mound if you can help it; 1/2 cup (45g) gives flavor and helps emulsify. The egg yolk makes the sauce silkier. Use pasteurized eggs. If you omit the egg yolk, add an extra 1/4 cup Parmesan and a little more butter; it will still work, just a touch less glossy. Season with Diamond Crystal kosher salt and black pepper. Salt matters because pasta water should taste like a lightly seasoned broth, not seawater.

## Instructions

I like to do this in a wide skillet with a pot of pasta nearby. The sauce is built in the same pan as the aromatics, so the timing is short and the cleanup stays reasonable.

### Step 1: Boil and salt the pasta

Bring 2 quarts (1.9L) water to a boil, then salt it. I use 1 tablespoon Diamond Crystal kosher salt; the water should taste like a light soup, not the ocean. Add 6 ounces pasta and cook until al dente. Before draining, scoop out 1/2 cup (120ml) pasta water. That water is the sauce. The starch in it lets butter, cheese, and egg cling to the pasta instead of sliding off into a puddle.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Measure the pasta water. If you drain blindly, you will add too much liquid later and the sauce will thin. Start with the reserved cup, not a stream.

### Step 2: Sear the chicken

Pat 4 ounces chicken breast cubes dry. Place 1 tablespoon olive oil and 1 tablespoon butter in a skillet over medium-high heat. Add chicken in a single layer. Let it sit for 1 minute so the pan forms a thin crust, then turn. Cook until the internal temperature reaches 165°F / 74°C and the pieces are golden at the edges. Transfer chicken to a small plate and cover loosely. Resting keeps the juices from running into the sauce too early.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Do not overcrowd. With 4 ounces for two, the pieces need room. If you scale to four servings, sear the chicken in two batches; otherwise it steams, and the color fades.

### Step 3: Build the spinach base

Squeeze the thawed spinach hard in a clean towel or your hand. This step is unglamorous, but wet spinach makes a pale, loose sauce. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon butter to the empty pan. Cook 1/4 cup finely diced onion until soft and translucent, about 2 minutes. Add 2 cloves minced garlic for 20 seconds, until fragrant but not browned. Stir in the spinach and 1/4 cup reserved pasta water. Cook until the spinach is heated through and glossy, about 1 minute.

### Step 4: Temper the egg yolk

In a small bowl, whisk 1 pasteurized egg yolk with 2 tablespoons pasta water. Slowly add 2 tablespoons of the hot spinach mixture while whisking, then repeat until the yolk has been warmed. Return the pan to the lowest heat setting and whisk in the tempered egg mixture. Keep stirring gently. The goal is a sauce that coats the back of a spoon. If you are using unpasteurized eggs, the FDA guidance is to cook to 160°F / 71°C; with pasteurized eggs you can keep the temperature lower, around 140°F to 150°F (60°C to 66°C), for silkiness.

Standalone wisdom: A hot pan can scramble an egg yolk in two seconds. Temperature control, not equipment, makes the difference.

Chef Augustin's Tip: If the sauce starts to look grainy, remove the pan from the burner and stir in 1 tablespoon pasta water. The starch can bring a slightly broken emulsion back, but if the pan is too hot, do not chase it with more cheese.

### Step 5: Fold in pasta and cheese

Add the drained pasta, 1/2 cup finely grated Parmesan, and chicken. Toss with tongs over low heat. Add pasta water 1 tablespoon at a time until the sauce is glossy and clings to each piece. The pasta should steam for 30 to 60 seconds, just long enough to bring the sauce to about 150°F / 65°C and the chicken back to 165°F / 74°C. Taste and season with salt and pepper.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Parmesan melts faster when it is finely grated. If you only have coarse grated cheese, add it in two additions and give the pasta a little more time. It will still work, just less instantly glossy.

### Step 6: Rest before serving

Plate and serve immediately. The sauce thickens as it cools, so if it sits more than 2 minutes, loosen it with a teaspoon of warm pasta water. Do not drown it—just bring it back to the coat.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong

Most creamy spinach pasta recipes I have tried either use too much frozen spinach or add it without squeezing. The result is a sauce that tastes good at the start of the meal and becomes watery at the halfway point. I also see recipes that use cream from the beginning. That can work, but for two it leaves you with a half carton and a heaviness that masks the garlic and Parmesan. My version uses a small amount of emulsified egg yolk instead, so the sauce has body without the dairy weight. Another gap: chicken is often cut too large, then boiled in the sauce until gray. For two people, 1/2-inch dice gives every bite a piece of protein, and the chicken reaches 165°F / 74°C quickly while the sauce is still coming together. The last mistake is seasoning at the end. Pasta sauce needs salt in the cooking water, salt on the chicken, and salt in the pan. If you wait until the plate, the cheese and spinach stay muted.

## Chef's Tips & What I've Learned

Starchy pasta water is a tool, not a leftover.
Squeeze frozen spinach until your hand aches.
Use a small bowl for tempering egg yolks; a giant bowl hides the yolk and makes it easy to lose temperature control.
A wide skillet beats a tall saucepan for two. Tall pans trap steam and make the chicken gray before it colors.
If you want a vegetarian version, use roasted mushrooms in place of chicken and skip the meat temperature step, but keep the sauce technique unchanged. If you omit the egg yolk, use extra butter and Parmesan; it will still work.
I have tested this with both stainless steel and cast iron. Cast iron wins because it holds more heat and gives the chicken a cleaner crust, while stainless is easier for deglazing the sauce base with pasta water.
When you bring plates to the table, leave one fork resting on the edge of the pasta bowl, not beside it. For two, the first bite matters more than the presentation, and a fork already in the bowl invites the other person to dig in before the sauce has a chance to set into a dull film.

## Questions People Ask About Creamy Spinach Pasta for Two

### How do I make creamy spinach pasta for two without cream?

Use butter, Parmesan, starchy pasta water, and a pasteurized egg yolk. The egg yolk provides lecithin, which helps fat and water cling together. Start with 3 tablespoons butter and 1/2 cup finely grated Parmesan. If you skip the egg yolk, add an extra 1/4 cup Parmesan and toss over low heat. The sauce will still coat the pasta, just with a slightly lighter body.

### Can I use ground beef instead of chicken breast?

Yes. Brown 4 ounces (115g) ground beef with the onion until it reaches 160°F / 71°C. USDA guidance for ground beef is 160°F / 71°C. Drain any excess fat before adding the spinach. Ground beef makes the dish deeper and savory; keep the butter at 2 tablespoons instead of 3 so the sauce does not become too heavy.

### What should I serve with creamy spinach pasta for two?

I pair it with something crisp and acidic: thinly sliced cucumber with lemon, a small tomato salad, or roasted green beans. The pasta is rich, so the side should be light in texture, not necessarily light in richness. For two, one side and one fruit is enough. Simple apple slices or grapefruit segments keep the meal feeling complete without adding another pot to the cleanup list.

### How long does creamy spinach pasta for two last in the fridge?

It keeps for about 3 days in a covered container at 40°F / 4°C or colder. Reheat it slowly in a skillet over low heat, adding 1 to 2 tablespoons pasta water or broth. If it separates, do not panic; a quick toss with the liquid usually rebinds the starch and cheese.

### Can you freeze creamy spinach pasta for two?

I would not freeze it after the sauce is made. USDA guidance says frozen food kept at 0°F / -18°C stays safe indefinitely, but texture is the issue here. The egg yolk emulsion and Parmesan can break when thawed, leaving a grainy texture. For make-ahead, freeze cooked pasta separately without sauce, and prep the spinach and chicken fresh on the day you plan to eat it. That gives you the same speed without a sad Tuesday plate.

### What are common mistakes when making creamy spinach pasta for two?

The biggest one is using wet spinach. The second is adding all the pasta water at once. The third is cooking the egg yolk over high heat, which scrambles it instead of enriching the sauce. A fourth is seasoning only after plating. Season the water, season the chicken, and taste before serving. These are small, boring adjustments, but they make the difference between a weeknight plate and something you will cook again.

# One-Pan Gnocchi for Two: 30-Minute Tomato-Basil Dinner

A skillet that starts with sizzling gnocchi and ends with a tomato sauce built from a can, an onion, and a handful of frozen vegetables is my default Tuesday-night dinner for two. I have made this vegetarian one-pan gnocchi for two enough times to know the two things that matter: get a real golden crust before liquid hits the pan, and use enough starchy tomato broth to build a sauce without drowning the dumplings. Most recipes I have tried either boil gnocchi in water first or pack a sheet pan full of sauce, then wonder why the dish turns soft. This version skips the boiling pot, keeps cleanup in one skillet, and makes pantry staples taste deliberate. The angle is simple: crisp the gnocchi in butter and oil, deglaze with reserved tomato juice, then simmer just long enough for the sauce to cling. It comes together in 30 minutes, and two portions can sit on a small table while the pan is still warm. If your stove runs hot, lower the heat for the simmer; if it runs gentle, give the sauce an extra minute to reduce.

## Why This Works
The magic here is texture management. Gnocchi are delicate: the potato or semolina surface has enough starch to brown, but it also absorbs liquid quickly. When I sear the gnocchi first in olive oil and butter, the outside firms up, giving them a thin crust that survives a short simmer. The butter contributes milk solids that caramelize slightly, while the oil keeps the surface from scorching too fast. That is one reason I prefer this technique to straight boiling. The onion and garlic then cook in the same fond, building a base that does not need anything else to taste full. Tomato paste, stirred for a minute, deepens its sweetness. Deglazing with reserved tomato juice and vegetable broth picks up the browned bits, which are the flavor anchors of the dish. I keep frozen vegetables near the end so they stay crisp-tender instead of releasing too much water. The final splash of butter at the end emulsifies the sauce and glosses the gnocchi without making them heavy.

I follow FDA advice for perishable dairy: keep cold items at or below 40°F / 4°C. For prepared leftovers, USDA guidance says to reheat to 165°F / 74°C throughout. That temperature line is why I do not leave a finished skillet sitting in a warm kitchen if I am not serving it immediately. The same logic is why I prefer low-sodium broth: I can season gradually instead of trying to rescue an oversalted pan.

A sauce is just fat, liquid, and patience arguing politely.

## Ingredients
The ingredients list is intentionally small, because a short list is easier to keep stocked for two. The 8 ounces (225g) of shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi is half of a 16-ounce package, which prevents leftovers that become gummy by Thursday. Olive oil carries the first browning; unsalted butter adds richness and lets me control salt. Onion and garlic are the aromatic foundation, and I mince the garlic late enough that it does not burn. Canned diced tomatoes are the body of the sauce, while tomato paste adds concentrated sweetness. Frozen mixed vegetables, usually peas, corn, and carrots, turn this into a full plate without requiring three extra chopping tasks. Low-sodium vegetable broth gives me room to season. Dried oregano, kosher salt, black pepper, and basil finish the flavor.

I rely on canned diced tomatoes because USDA commercial canning guidance keeps them shelf-stable before opening; once opened, I refrigerate them within 2 hours, following FDA advice. If fresh herbs are scarce, substitute 1/2 teaspoon dried basil for fresh basil, but add it earlier with the oregano so it has time to soften. If you want more body, stir in 1/2 cup (120g) drained cooked cannellini beans with the tomatoes. If your frozen vegetables include leafy spinach, add them with the gnocchi rather than at the end so they wilt. Either way, it will still work.

## Instructions
Use a 10-inch skillet if you can; it gives the gnocchi room to brown and the sauce room to reduce. The steps move quickly, so have the diced onion, garlic, tomato paste, and frozen vegetables beside the stove.

### Step 1: Sear the Gnocchi
Pat the gnocchi dry with paper towels. Heat olive oil and half the butter in a 10-inch skillet over medium-high heat. Once the butter foams and smells nutty, add the gnocchi in a single layer. Leave them alone for 2 minutes, then shake the pan, turn the pieces, and sear 1 to 2 minutes more until golden. (If your pan is smaller than 10 inches, do this in two batches; crowding turns browning into steaming.)

The goal is color, not boiled softness. A golden patch means the surface has tightened and is less likely to dissolve during simmering.

### Step 2: Soften the Onion
Move the browned gnocchi to a bowl. Reduce heat to medium, add diced onion and a pinch of kosher salt, and cook until the onion is glossy and beginning to taste sweet, about 2 to 3 minutes. Add garlic and cook for another 30 seconds, until fragrant.

This aromatic step is where the dish starts tasting like dinner rather than canned food. The salt helps draw moisture from the onion and keeps the pan from drying out.

### Step 3: Brown the Tomato Paste
Push the onion and garlic to one side and add tomato paste to the empty space. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the paste darkens from bright red to brick red and clings to the pan in small patches, about 1 minute. Mix it into the aromatics.

I do not rush this; raw tomato paste can taste metallic, while cooked paste adds rounded sweetness.

### Step 4: Deglaze with Tomato Juice and Broth
Pour in reserved tomato juice and vegetable broth. Scrape the browned bits from the bottom with a wooden spoon or silicone spatula. Let the liquid bubble briskly for about 1 minute, so the acidity lifts the caramel and reduces slightly.

At this point I taste the thin sauce. If it needs salt, I wait until the tomatoes go in, because the tomato liquid will concentrate as it simmers.

### Step 5: Simmer with Tomatoes and Frozen Vegetables
Add drained tomatoes, dried oregano, black pepper, and frozen mixed vegetables. Return the gnocchi to the pan, nestling them into the sauce without fully covering each piece. Bring to a gentle simmer, then cook until the gnocchi are tender and the sauce clings, 5 to 7 minutes for shelf-stable gnocchi or 3 minutes for fresh gnocchi. (If the sauce looks loose, simmer uncovered another minute; if it looks tight, add another 1 to 2 tablespoons of broth.)

The dish is done when the sauce can coat the back of a spoon and the gnocchi feel tender with a slight chew. Stop a little early if they seem close, because residual heat continues softening them.

### Step 6: Finish with Butter and Basil
Take the pan off the heat and stir in the remaining butter until glossy. Add basil, taste, and adjust salt. (Cold butter at the end gives body without the heaviness that comes from cooking all the butter in one step.)

Let the skillet rest for 1 minute so the sauce settles, then divide the gnocchi between two shallow bowls.

## What Most Recipes Get Wrong
The mistake I keep seeing is skipping the sear and throwing everything into liquid. That produces soft gnocchi and a sauce that tastes flat. The other common error is using too much broth for a two-person portion. 3/4 cup is usually plenty for 8 ounces of gnocchi, especially when the tomatoes release juice. I learned this after several watery Tuesday dinners. Now I start with 3/4 cup broth and only add more if the sauce looks tight.

Because this is a one-pan meal, crowding matters. If the gnocchi are piled high, they steam instead of browning. A 10-inch skillet gives enough room for the crust to set before sauce arrives. Another fix is timing the frozen vegetables. They can go in late so they heat through and retain snap. If you add them at the beginning [with tomatoes](/recipes/whole30-chicken-skillet-tomatoes-garlic), they turn dull.

I also keep the final simmer uncovered. If the pan is crowded with sauce, the gnocchi soften too much and the tomato flavor stays sharp. A small simmer reduces acidity and lets the basil look brighter. Since gnocchi continue to soften after cooking, stop a little early if they seem close.

## Chef's Tips & What I have Learned
Chef Augustin's Tip: Use an unscented neutral oil if your butter browns too quickly in your particular skillet. Cast iron and carbon steel can run hotter than nonstick, and the butter solids need protection. The why matters: oil raises the scorch resistance while butter still supplies flavor.

Chef Augustin's Tip: Drain canned tomatoes but reserve the juice. The juice deglazes with acidity and a little sweetness, while the drained tomato solids prevent the sauce from becoming soup. (If you are in a hurry, pulse the tomatoes with their juice, but add 2 fewer tablespoons of broth.)

Do not rinse the tomatoes; draining leaves enough pulp to thicken. I follow FDA guidance for butter and other soft dairy: keep it cold until needed, and do not let it sit out for more than 2 hours when the room is warm. For leftover reheating, warm the portion gently until steaming; USDA guidance for reheating prepared leftovers is 165°F / 74°C.

A well-made sauce should coat, not swim.

If you want a richer finish without opening a can of cream, stir in a small piece of cold butter off the heat. It coats the gnocchi and rounds the tomato acidity. For texture, a small sprinkle of toasted breadcrumbs over the finished bowls adds a second kind of crispness; use a dry skillet and about 1 minute of attention.

## FAQ
### How much gnocchi for two people?
Start with 8 ounces (225g) shelf-stable or refrigerated potato gnocchi. That is half a 16-ounce package, enough for two main portions when paired with tomato sauce, onion, garlic, and frozen vegetables. I like this number because it leaves room for browning; too many dumplings pile up and steam instead of crisping. If your eaters are hungrier, use 10 to 12 ounces (285g to 340g), add a splash more broth, and simmer 1 extra minute. If serving beside salad, stay at 8 ounces.

### Can you make gnocchi for two in one pan?
Yes. Use a 10-inch skillet and treat one pan as the whole system: brown the gnocchi, build the onion, garlic, and tomato paste base in the same pan, deglaze, then simmer everything together. Keep the sauce shallow enough that the gnocchi can move a little. A 9-inch skillet works for two if you stir gently. This is easier than boiling because gnocchi starch thickens the tomato sauce directly in the pan.

### How do I make a one-pan gnocchi dinner vegetarian?
Keep olive oil and butter as the base, use vegetable broth, and add frozen vegetables for color and bite. The tomato, garlic, onion, and basil combo already has depth, especially when tomato paste browns. For more body, stir in 1/2 cup (120g) drained cooked cannellini beans with the tomatoes. For gloss, finish with a knob of cold butter off heat. Keep the pantry staples: canned tomatoes, dried oregano, black pepper, and Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

### What are common gnocchi cooking mistakes?
The most common mistake is overcooking before the skillet. Shelf-stable or refrigerated gnocchi cook quickly, so they need only a sear and a few minutes of simmering. Another error is skipping the dry-off step, which prevents browning. Overcrowding is the third: too many dumplings piled up steam into soft pillows. I also watch sauce quantity; too much broth makes a thin soup. Add basil and frozen vegetables late so they keep flavor and color.

### How do I scale a one-pan gnocchi recipe for two?
For two servings, keep the structure simple: 8 ounces (225g) gnocchi, 1/2 cup (75g) diced onion, 2 garlic cloves, 1/4 cup (48g) tomato paste, 1 drained can of diced tomatoes, and 3/4 cup (180ml) broth. For four, use 16 ounces (450g) gnocchi and increase the sauce by half, not double, in a 12-inch skillet. For one, use 4 ounces (115g) gnocchi and 6 to 8 tablespoons (90ml) broth. Scaling works because the technique stays the same.

At the table, two bowls are full enough that a spoon stays upright, basil is scattered over glossy [tomato sauce](/recipes/one-pan-chicken-rice-garlic-butter-tomato-sauce), and the skillet is still warm enough to make the house smell like garlic as the first bites arrive.
